synopsis: The corpus found no off-road document accepting simulation as compliance evidence, no precedent for regulatory or notified-body acceptance of off-road collision-avoidance simulation, and no published criteria resolving how much virtual evidence would be accepted [f167, f7417, f10307]. On-road acceptance provides a limited precedent under strict credibility rules: UNECE NATM uses virtual testing within a wider assessment, and even the most simulation-friendly EU automated-driving regime does not allow simulation to substitute for physical tests [f168, f7679, f10410]. For an EU machine introduced in mid-2027, Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027 and requires risk reduction, safe and reliable controls, and technical conformity evidence; every Annex I Part A conformity route involves a notified body, including the listed category of self-evolving machine-learning safety components [f2201, f2202, f363, f794]. Standards compliance is not equivalent to legal compliance, and UL 4600, ISO 34502 and NASA guidance provide safety-case or methodological help rather than off-road conformity routes [f2146, f12267, f449, f8070]. Formal approval is a hard calendar constraint, the proposed braking function's regulatory route remains unconfirmed, and the booklet recommends jurisdiction-specific legal and conformity planning now rather than legal review at the end of validation [f360, f10499, f10702, f10848].
